source: Newton's Third Law
Forces come in pairs: when A pushes B, B pushes A just as hard in the opposite direction.
Students think the bigger or faster object pushes harder in a collision.
Push on a wall and you feel it push back on your hands. That is not a coincidence. Every force is half of an interaction between two objects, and the other half is always there.
Newton's third law: when object A pushes on object B, B pushes on A with a force of the same size in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different objects.

A force is an interaction, like a handshake: you can't shake hands without the other hand shaking yours. When a bug hits a car's windshield, the windshield pushes on the bug and the bug pushes on the windshield, with equal force. The results look different only because the same force does much more to a tiny bug than to a heavy car.
Two blocks pushed together. Each third-law pair shares a color: the forces are equal and opposite, and each one acts on a different block.
A skater pushes a wall with 90 N. What force does the wall exert on the skater?
Pushing off
90 N, pushing the skater away from the wall
The pair to "skater pushes wall" is "wall pushes skater."
Same size, opposite direction: 90 N, away from the wall.
That push is what sends the skater gliding backward.
What pushes a rocket upward when it takes off?
A rocket
The exhaust gas, pushing back on the rocket
The rocket pushes hot exhaust gas down out of its nozzle.
By the third law, the gas pushes the rocket up just as hard.
No air is needed, which is why rockets work in space.

Thinking the bigger or faster object pushes harder in a collision. In a crash between a truck and a small car, each pushes the other with exactly the same force. The small car is damaged more because the same force gives its smaller mass a bigger acceleration. Check: third-law pairs are always equal, whatever the masses or speeds.
